title: Summer and Letters
premise: Gideon Almeida has spent eleven years on a small Atlantic island counting sea turtles and keeping their heart carefully archived, ever since the summer their first love, Marisol Vega, vanished without a word. When a storm uncovers a letter Marisol mailed in the final week of that summer—never delivered, postmarked eleven years ago—Gideon learns the disappearance was engineered by Marisol's powerful family, who saw Gideon as a threat to their empire. Marisol returns to the island to settle her dying father's estate, and the two are forced to excavate the truth: the letter, the lies, and the loyalty that kept them both silent. As the Vega family closes ranks to bury what Gideon has uncovered, Gideon must choose between the safe invisibility they've built and testifying to what really happened—choosing truth and love together, even as Marisol's father's final days and the family's lawyers race to silence them first.
about_author: Cyrus Lockridge is the pen name of a former coastal field researcher who traded tide charts for manuscripts after a decade of island postings. Their fiction is known for slow-burning romances set against working waterfronts, where the sea keeps better secrets than people do.

chapters.title: Nest Count
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Opening on the eleventh nesting season since Marisol disappeared, Gideon runs the island's turtle survey with practiced detachment, counting nests the way they count the years. A routine morning establishes their careful, self-contained life. Emotional beat: the quiet ache of a person who has organized grief into data.

chapters.title: What the Storm Brought Up
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A nor'easter scours the dunes and exposes an old storm drain near the Vega property. Gideon finds a water-swollen envelope wedged in the debris—addressed to them in handwriting they'd know anywhere, postmarked eleven years ago. Emotional beat: the past physically surfacing, refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with flashback. Alone in the field station, Gideon reads Marisol's letter: she was being sent away, her father had discovered them, she begged Gideon to meet her at the boathouse the night she vanished. Gideon never got it. The chapter ends with Gideon learning the Vega estate is being settled—and Marisol is coming back. Emotional beat: eleven years of self-blame collapsing in one evening.

chapters.title: The Heir Returns
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol lands on the island to inventory her dying father's holdings, all business, all armor. She's spent a decade as the obedient Vega, engaged to a merger of a marriage. Seeing the island—and hearing Gideon's name from the ferry pilot—cracks the composure. Emotional beat: the cost of a life built on someone else's terms.

chapters.title: Tide Pools
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. A forced encounter at the survey beach: Marisol came to see the turtles she remembers; Gideon came to work. They circle each other with eleven years of unspoken things, civility stretched thin. Marisol notices Gideon wears the same worn field watch she gave them. Emotional beat: recognition underneath the estrangement.

chapters.title: Boathouse Ghosts
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon finally asks the question they've carried: why the boathouse, why no note, why nothing. Marisol, blindsided—she left a letter—realizes her letter never arrived and that Gideon has spent eleven years believing they were abandoned. She can't yet explain who intercepted it. Emotional beat: two people discovering they were both lied to.

chapters.title: The Father's House
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol sorts her father's study and finds a locked drawer of correspondence—her own confiscated letters, including the draft of one she never mailed, and a legal file labeled 'Almeida.' Her father, lucid in a rare moment, warns her to let the past stay past. Emotional beat: the machinery of her family's control coming into view.

chapters.title: Salt and Small Truths
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Gideon and Marisol fall back into an old rhythm during night surveys—checking nests together, talking in the dark where it's easier. They trade small truths: her hollow engagement, their self-imposed exile. Neither names what's rekindling. Emotional beat: intimacy rebuilding in the dark, piece by careful piece.

chapters.title: The File Labeled Almeida
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol opens the drawer's legal file: her father's lawyers documented Gideon for years—photos, the survey grant they quietly tried to revoke, the letter intercepted and filed as evidence of 'leverage.' She realizes her family didn't just separate them; they ran surveillance on a teenager. Emotional beat: loyalty to family curdling into horror.

chapters.title: What Gideon Knew
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Flashback chapter to the final summer: the threats the Vegas made, the survey funding pulled, Gideon's mother's job quietly threatened—details Gideon never connected until now. Present-day Gideon realizes the pattern never stopped. Emotional beat: the past tense breaking open; invisibility was engineered, not chosen.

chapters.title: Confluence
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Marisol tells Gideon everything: the intercepted letter, the file, the surveillance. Gideon's relief at not being abandoned collides with fury that Marisol stayed silent for a decade. First real fight—and first real honesty. They admit the love never left. Emotional beat: truth as both wound and hinge.

chapters.title: The Executor
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The family's longtime lawyer, Mr. Sandoval, arrives to 'assist' with the estate—and makes clear he knows Marisol has been in the study. He hints that the dying father's legacy, and Marisol's inheritance, depend on discretion. Meanwhile Gideon's grant renewal is inexplicably flagged. Emotional beat: the old machinery waking up, aimed at both of them.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The survey station loses its lease—Vega-owned property, 'sold to new interests.' Gideon's colleagues urge them to drop whatever's spooked the family. Gideon, who spent eleven years being invisible to survive, feels the old fear and refuses it for the first time. Emotional beat: the moment retreat stops being an option.

chapters.title: The Unsent Letter
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds the letter she never mailed at nineteen—the one where she chose to obey her father—and finally gives it to Gideon, unfinished and damning. Gideon reads her surrender in her own teenage handwriting. It hurts more than the lie. Emotional beat: the full weight of what loyalty to the wrong power cost them both.

chapters.title: Nest at Risk
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. A construction crew arrives to begin 'shoreline remediation'—directly over an active nesting beach, mid-season. It's legal, permitted, and timed to punish. Gideon files an emergency objection and goes public with the ecological stakes. Emotional beat: Gideon choosing to be seen, loudly, for the first time.

chapters.title: Sandoval's Offer
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Sandoval meets Gideon privately: withdraw the objection, return the letter's existence to silence, and the station lease is restored—plus a generous endowment. He makes explicit what was always implicit: the family buried the letter once and can bury Gideon's career again. Emotional beat: corruption offering a comfortable cage.

chapters.title: The Dying Man's Confession
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. At her father's deathbed, Marisol demands the truth. He gives it in fragments: he intercepted the letter, he bought Gideon's silence through pressure he told himself was protection. He asks—not orders—her not to destroy the family. She realizes he's asking her to become him. Emotional beat: grief and refusal arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol weighs everything: her inheritance, her name, her engagement, her mother's fragile peace—against a folder of evidence and a person she loves. She breaks the engagement, knowing the financial and social fallout will be immediate and vicious. Emotional beat: loyalty finally redirected toward truth instead of power.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Climax. At the coastal commission hearing on the nesting beach, Gideon testifies—and Marisol walks in and corroborates, submitting the file, the intercepted letter, and her own sworn statement about the family's decades of interference. Sandoval's counterattack collapses as her father, hours from death, signs an affidavit confirming everything. Emotional beat: the whole heart risked in public, together.

chapters.title: After the Verdict
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The objection is upheld; the beach is protected; the Vega machine, exposed, retreats into settlement talks. But victory feels strange—Gideon has lost the station's quiet anonymity and gained a life under lights. Marisol, disinherited and unmoored, wonders aloud if she has anything to offer but wreckage. Emotional beat: the vulnerable aftermath of courage.

chapters.title: Hatchlings
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Hatchling season peaks. On the beach at dawn, they watch hundreds of turtles make for the water—small, exposed, and going anyway. Marisol has taken a lease on the old boathouse; Gideon has offered her a job on the survey, and a drawer, and a key. Emotional beat: love chosen in daylight, without conditions.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, closing. A year later: the station is community-run, Marisol is cataloguing the Vega papers into an archive that keeps the family honest, and a new letter sits on the field desk—Gideon's own, written to their younger self, finally answerable. They stop counting years and start counting nests again, this time with someone beside them. Emotional beat: the heart taken out of the past tense, for good.
